strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: conformal prediction in extremely long-tailed settings (up to 8,142 classes), where existing class-conditional CP methods (CLASSWISE, Clustered CP, rank-calibrated CP) fail due to scarce calibration data per class.

Approach I is theoretically grounded and novel: the authors derive oracle-optimal sets for a new target (macro-coverage) via the Neyman-Pearson lemma, showing that thresholding p(y|x)/p(y) optimally trades off expected set size and macro-coverage, and turn this into a practical score (PAS) that retains a marginal coverage guarantee. The weighted-macro-coverage extension (WPAS) applied to IUCN at-risk species is a nice, application-relevant generalization.

Approach II is principled rather than ad hoc: FUZZY CP is framed as label-weighted conformal prediction, with a formal proposition (with proof) that the bandwidth interpolates between CLASSWISE and STANDARD CP, and a reconformalization step (plus a full-conformal variant in the appendix) that restores a marginal coverage guarantee.

Comprehensive evaluation on realistic benchmarks (Pl@ntNet-300K, iNaturalist 2018, plus truncated versions for reliable class-conditional estimation), against relevant baselines including Exact Classwise and Clustered CP from Ding et al. (2023), with sensible metrics (FracBelow50%, UnderCovGap, MacroCov, marginal coverage, set size).

The simulated human decision-maker study (expert verifier vs. random guesser vs. mixtures) connects coverage/size trade-offs to downstream decision accuracy, which strengthens the practical significance beyond abstract coverage numbers.
Transparent reporting of assumptions and limitations (e.g., double use of the val set, degenerate behavior on balanced data), with clear discussion of how parameters can be tuned in practice.
weaknesses: Limited methodological depth/incrementality: PAS reduces to inverse-prevalence weighting of the softmax score, an idea closely related to label-shift importance weighting (e.g., Podkopaev & Ramdas, 2021, acknowledged), and Approach II is a fairly natural interpolation of existing weighted-CP machinery. The theory mainly re-applies the Neyman-Pearson lemma.

The gap between oracle optimality (Proposition 1/4, which requires true p(y|x) and p(y)) and the practical method (using imperfect estimates) is not quantified; there is no bound or empirical investigation of how estimation error in p̂(y) degrades macro-coverage optimality.

The class mapping Π_prevalence is heuristic and may be brittle: grouping classes by prevalence is a weak proxy for score-distribution similarity, and the more principled Π_quantile mapping actually underperforms both Π_prevalence and Π_random (Figure 6), raising questions about the robustness of FUZZY CP to the mapping choice.

Evaluation robustness concerns: only two datasets, one backbone (ResNet-50), one score family (softmax), and apparently single runs with no error bars or confidence intervals; statistical uncertainty in per-class coverage estimates for rare classes is not addressed.

The simulated decision-maker analysis is simplistic (expert verifier who is always correct, uniform random guesser); no human study or more realistic user models are used despite the strong claims about downstream utility.

Reproducibility is weakened: the code availability statement in Section 3 is literally 'available at' with no URL, and the paper relies on nontrivial dataset re-splitting (iNaturalist) and bandwidth grid choices that would be hard to reproduce exactly.

METHODS guarantee only marginal coverage; class-conditional benefits are purely empirical, so the central claim of improved coverage of rare classes rests entirely on the experiments, which are consistent but not accompanied by significance testing.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically important problem: conformal prediction in extreme long-tailed settings (1,000–8,000 classes), where class-conditional coverage is hard to achieve with few calibration examples per class.

The theoretical framing is clean: Proposition 4 derives oracle-optimal prediction sets for (weighted) macro-coverage via the Neyman-Pearson lemma, and the PAS score function (thresholding p̂(y|x)/p̂(y)) is a natural and well-motivated approximation of these oracle sets that inherits the marginal coverage guarantee.

FUZZY CP is a principled interpolation between STANDARD and CLASSWISE CP via label-weighted conformal prediction, with a reconformalization step (Proposition 3) that provably restores marginal coverage; a full-conformal variant avoiding data splitting is also provided (Proposition 6). Proposition 5 rigorously shows Raw FUZZY recovers both extremes as the bandwidth varies.

The evaluation is comprehensive: two real long-tailed benchmarks (Pl@ntNet-300K, iNaturalist), both natural and truncated versions, multiple coverage/size metrics, several relevant baselines (STANDARD, CLASSWISE, EXACT CLASSWISE, CLUSTERED), ablations over the class mapping Π, a weighted macro-coverage extension for at-risk species, and a simulated human decision-maker study connecting coverage and set size to decision utility.

Code availability, detailed experimental setup in Appendix B, and honest discussion of limitations (e.g., exchangeability violation from reusing the validation set, inapplicability to balanced datasets) improve transparency and reproducibility.

The paper positions itself well against related work (Ding et al. 2023; Podkopaev & Ramdas 2021; Shi et al. 2024) and clearly articulates the distinction between its goals and prior class-conditional CP work.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate. The PAS score is a simple prevalence-normalized softmax, and its oracle optimality is a direct corollary of the Neyman-Pearson lemma (the paper itself acknowledges this lineage via Sadinle et al. 2019). FUZZY CP closely resembles label-dependent weighted CP from Podkopaev and Ramdas (2021), with the main addition being the reconformalization wrapper.

The key design choice behind FUZZY CP — mapping classes by their training prevalence (Π_prevalence) — is ad hoc and justified only heuristically. The ablation showing Π_prevalence beats Π_quantile and Π_random is suggestive but not a principled derivation, and it is unclear whether the method transfers to other modalities or classifier families where prevalence is not the dominant driver of score distributions.

Results are presented almost entirely through dense Pareto-frontier plots (Figures 4, 6, 7) without tables reporting exact numbers, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds. Given the noisy class-conditional coverage estimates for tail classes, quantitative uncertainty reporting would substantially strengthen the empirical claims.

The evaluation is limited to a single classifier architecture (ResNet-50, 20 epochs) and two image datasets. The claim that INTERP-Q 'lacks a guarantee but performs well' rests entirely on these settings, and no experiments with stronger or modern backbones are provided.

Practical validity concerns: the validation set is used both for model selection and as the calibration set, violating the exchangeability assumption in theory. The authors argue empirically it makes little difference (val vs. test q̂: 0.923 vs. 0.925), but this check is reported only for one method on one dataset.

The macro-coverage itself is not guaranteed — only marginal coverage is. The improved macro-coverage is purely empirical and depends on the accuracy of p̂(y) and p̂(y|x) in the tail, where both estimates are weakest; the paper does not analyze sensitivity to poor prevalence estimates.

The human decision-maker study (Section 3.2) is entirely simulated with stylized models (expert verifier, random guesser) and is restricted to truncated datasets; it therefore provides only weak evidence about real human-AI interaction benefits despite the strong practical motivation in the introduction.

Some presentation issues: the code URL in Section 3 is empty, Figure 4 is overloaded to the point of being difficult to read, and INTERP-Q's ad hoc treatment of infinite classwise quantiles (replacing ∞ with 1) is under-justified.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: class-conditional coverage of prediction sets in extreme long-tailed settings (thousands of classes with few calibration examples) is genuinely underexplored, and the paper articulates the fundamental trade-off between set size and class-conditional coverage convincingly.

Two complementary and principled contributions: (i) the macro-coverage objective with a Neyman-Pearson-based optimality analysis showing the PAS score is the natural prevalence-adjusted score function, and (ii) Fuzzy CP, which elegantly unifies Standard and Classwise CP as two extremes of label-weighted conformal prediction and adds a simple reconformalization step that provably restores marginal coverage.

Theoretical results are correct and well-integrated: the optimality of thresholding on p(y|x)/p(y) follows cleanly from the Neyman-Pearson lemma, the recovery of Standard/Classwise in the bandwidth limits of Raw Fuzzy is carefully proven (including the infinite-quantile edge case), and a full-conformal alternative to data splitting is provided.

Empirically strong evaluation: two large-scale long-tailed benchmarks (Pl@ntNet-300K with 1,081 classes, iNaturalist 2018 with 8,142 classes), full and truncated variants, multiple aggregate coverage metrics, strong baselines (Classwise, Exact Classwise, Clustered CP), sensitivity analyses over bandwidths, alternative class mappings, and a creative simulated human decision-maker study that connects coverage/size to decision accuracy.
Practical relevance is well argued, including a compelling Pl@ntNet case study on IUCN-listed endangered species and an extension (WPAS) to weighted macro-coverage; code is stated to be released.
Honest discussion of limitations, including the lack of guarantees for Interp-Q, the heuristic nature of the prevalence mapping, and the caveat that methods are not intended for balanced datasets.
weaknesses: Moderate conceptual novelty in places: label-weighted conformal prediction with label-dependent weights is established (Tibshirani et al., 2019; Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2021), and Fuzzy CP is essentially a careful instantiation of it plus a reconformalization wrapper; the optimality result is a direct application of the Neyman-Pearson lemma, so the technical depth is limited even if the framing is fresh.

The prevalence-based class mapping Π_prevalence is heuristic and only loosely justified (classes with similar prevalence need not have similar score distributions); the alternative Π_quantile mapping that directly targets score-distribution similarity performs worse, which the authors attribute to noise but do not resolve. The method's success appears partly tied to this ad hoc design choice.
Approach II only guarantees marginal coverage, not any form of class-conditional or macro coverage; the theoretical guidance for what Fuzzy CP actually optimizes is limited compared to Approach I.

Evaluation is confined to a single classifier architecture (ResNet-50) and two image datasets; no experiments on other modalities or with different backbones, so generality of the conclusions across model families is untested. The softmax score is assumed throughout, and interactions with APS/RAPS-type scores are not explored.

Some experimental hygiene concerns: the validation set is used both for model selection and as the conformal calibration set, which violates exchangeability; the authors argue this is negligible empirically, but a cleaner protocol with a dedicated calibration split would strengthen the guarantees, and the reconformalization holdout of 5,000 examples is a nontrivial data cost in the rare-class regime the paper targets.

Tuning burden (σ or τ) shifts the trade-off but requires the practitioner to pick an operating point; while tunable on the calibration set, the paper gives little guidance or automatic selection procedure, and the sensitivity analyses are confined to the appendix.

Figures 4-7 are dense and hard to parse (log-scale set sizes, overlapping sweeps over α and hyperparameters); a compact table quantifying improvements of the proposed methods over baselines at matched set sizes would make the headline claims easier to verify.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: conformal prediction for extremely long-tailed classification (1,000+ classes) where class-conditional coverage is difficult, with a compelling real-world motivation (Pl@ntNet, biodiversity monitoring, endangered species).

The macro-coverage target is a natural and previously unexplored relaxed notion of class-conditional coverage for this setting, and the paper derives the oracle-optimal set (via Neyman-Pearson) that balances set size and (weighted) macro-coverage, giving a principled basis for the proposed PAS/WPAS score functions.

Simple, practical methods (PAS, WPAS, INTERP-Q) that retain marginal coverage guarantees, are easy to implement, and empirically trace a useful size/coverage trade-off (e.g., halving the number of under-covered classes from 421 to 180 on Pl@ntNet-300K at only a modest size increase).

Extensive and careful experiments: two large-scale long-tailed datasets plus truncated versions for reliable class-conditional estimation, multiple relevant baselines (STANDARD, CLASSWISE, EXACT CLASSWISE, CLUSTERED), sensitivity analyses (focal loss, alternative FUZZY mappings), a simulated human decision-maker study, and released code.

Appendices are thorough: full proofs of the oracle results and of the 1−2α marginal coverage guarantee for INTERP-Q, a related FUZZY classwise method with reconformalization, and honest discussion of limitations (e.g., conservative theoretical bound, τ selection violating exchangeability).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: PAS is essentially a prevalence-normalized softmax score, closely related to logit adjustment for long-tail learning (Menon et al., 2021) and label-shift-corrected conformal scores (Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2021), and the oracle analysis is a direct application of the Neyman-Pearson lemma; the conceptual delta over these lines of work is incremental.

INTERP-Q is a very simple heuristic (linear interpolation of quantiles) with only a weak 1−2α marginal coverage guarantee; the procedure lacks any theoretical justification for its favorable class-conditional behavior, and the good empirical results depend on the sharp skew of softmax scores for rare classes.
Missing comparison against rank-calibrated class-conditional CP (Shi et al., 2024), which is explicitly cited as a relevant method for the many-class imbalanced setting.

The claim that STANDARD with PAS is 'Pareto optimal' is an empirical statement on two datasets and one model family (ResNet-50 with softmax score); the oracle optimality argument relies on accurate estimates of p(y|x) and p(y), which the paper acknowledges are imperfect, and results could degrade with a poorly calibrated classifier or other architectures.

The benefit of PAS over STANDARD is modest on iNaturalist-2018 (Table 4), suggesting the practical gains may be dataset-dependent; and rare-class class-conditional metrics on the full datasets are necessarily noisy, which somewhat weakens fine-grained conclusions.
Evaluation is restricted to image classification with a single backbone; generalization to other modalities, scores, and label distributions is not demonstrated.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely practical and underexplored problem: constructing prediction sets with good class-conditional (or macro-) coverage in extremely long-tailed settings with thousands of classes, where existing class-conditional conformal methods (CLASSWISE, CLUSTERED) degenerate to huge or vacuous sets.

The macro-coverage objective is a reasonable and clearly motivated relaxation of class-conditional coverage, and the oracle analysis (Proposition 1/2) via the Neyman-Pearson lemma correctly identifies the p(y|x)/p(y) ratio as the optimal thresholding statistic for the size/macro-coverage trade-off.

The empirical evaluation is fairly thorough: two large-scale long-tailed datasets (Pl@ntNet-300K, iNaturalist-2018) with thousands of classes, multiple coverage metrics, sensitivity to α, focal-loss variants, truncated-dataset ablations, and a simulated human decision-maker study connecting coverage/size to downstream decision accuracy.
The WPAS extension for prioritizing at-risk (e.g., endangered) species is a nice application-motivated touch, and the paper is generally well written with honest discussion of limitations.
The FRUZZY/label-weighted view in Appendix A connects INTERP-Q to weighted conformal prediction and includes a full-conformal alternative (Proposition 8).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The PAS score p̂(y|x)/p̂(y) is essentially prior-corrected/logit-adjusted softmax, a well-known technique in long-tailed learning (Menon et al., 2021, cited but not engaged with as a competing method); the oracle result is a direct application of the Neyman-Pearson lemma, and the paper itself cites the analogous marginal/classwise result from Sadinle et al. (2019).

INTERP-Q is a very simple heuristic (linear interpolation of two quantile vectors) with only a weak 1−2α marginal guarantee that is admittedly conservative; the interesting practical behavior (nonlinear set-size response to τ) is observed empirically but not analyzed or understood.

The empirical gains are modest and dataset-dependent: on iNaturalist-2018, STANDARD with PAS barely improves over STANDARD (FracBelow50% 0.058→0.042 at α=0.1), and meaningful class-coverage improvements from INTERP-Q require set sizes of 30–55 classes, raising questions about practical usefulness for the motivating human-verification use case.

The macro-coverage guarantee of PAS is only approximate and depends on the quality of p̂(y) estimated from training-label prevalences; the paper provides no theory or experiments quantifying how estimation error in the tail (where p(y)→0) degrades the approximation, which seems central to the long-tailed claim.

Baseline coverage is thin: no comparison to methods combining logit adjustment with conformal prediction, no adaptive/recalibration approaches targeting tail coverage, and the human decision-maker study uses synthetic verifier models rather than any real user data despite the human-centered motivation.

The framing risks conflating conformal validity with utility: improved macro-coverage under exchangeability says little about behavior under the distribution shift that naturally occurs in citizen-science deployment, which the broader-impacts discussion implicitly relies on.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: conformal prediction in extremely long-tailed, many-class settings (1,081 and 8,142 classes) is underexplored, and the trade-off between set size and class-conditional coverage is convincingly framed with a concrete application (biodiversity monitoring, Pl@ntNet).

The macro-coverage target (average of class-conditional coverages) is a natural and previously unexplored relaxation, and the paper derives the oracle-optimal set form via the Neyman-Pearson lemma, giving a principled (if simple) derivation of the PAS score p(y|x)/p(y) and its weighted variant WPAS.

Honest and transparent about guarantees: PAS inherits only marginal coverage, INTERP-Q has a 1-2α bound (shown to be conservative), and the paper openly discusses limitations such as the exchangeability violation when tuning τ.

Thorough empirical evaluation: two real long-tailed datasets plus truncated variants, multiple coverage metrics (FracBelow50%, UnderCovGap, MacroCov, MarginalCov), several baselines (Standard, Classwise, Clustered, Exact Classwise), ablations (focal loss, different FUZZY mappings, combined PAS+INTERP-Q), and a simulated human decision-maker study connecting coverage/size to downstream decision accuracy.
The appendix contains complete proofs, a well-specified experimental setup, and code for reproduction; the WPAS extension for prioritizing at-risk species is a nice practical touch.

Results are convincing: e.g., PAS roughly halves the number of badly under-covered classes at nearly no set-size cost, and the INTERP-Q trade-off analysis (nonlinear set-size response to τ) is insightful.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty of the main tools: the PAS score p(y|x)/p(y) is essentially the quantity underlying logit adjustment (Menon et al., 2021, cited but not deeply engaged), and the paper does not compare against the natural baseline of standard CP applied to a logit-adjusted / prevalence-rebalanced classifier, which may achieve similar class-conditional coverage improvements. INTERP-Q is a very simple linear interpolation of quantile thresholds.

The theoretical guarantees are modest: PAS provides only marginal coverage (the macro-coverage optimality is for oracle sets and depends on the accuracy of p̂(y|x) and p̂(y) estimated from training labels), and the INTERP-Q 1-2α bound is a trivial union bound; no theory quantifies how close the realized trade-off is to the oracle Pareto frontier.

Experiments are restricted to a single architecture (ResNet-50), a single score family (softmax-based; APS/RAPS are dismissed without empirical comparison), and simulated rather than real human studies, so the practical claim about decision-maker utility remains partially unverified.
Estimating p̂(y) from training data may be unreliable when class distributions shift between deployment and calibration; sensitivity to this estimate is not analyzed.
The FUZZY method, although theoretically cleaner (1-α marginal coverage), empirically does not outperform the simpler INTERP-Q, which somewhat dilutes the contribution of Appendix A.
Claims such as 'STANDARD with PAS is Pareto optimal' are empirical observations over the tested methods, not provable properties, and the wording occasionally overstates what the evidence shows.
